abstract: This NBER working paper constructs an occupation-level adaptive capacity index measuring workers' ability to navigate job transitions if displaced by AI, covering 356 occupations representing 95.9% of the US workforce. The index combines net liquid wealth, skill transferability, geographic density, and age. The central finding is that AI exposure and adaptive capacity are positively correlated (r=0.502): most workers in highly AI-exposed occupations are well-positioned to adapt. However, 6.1 million workers (4.2%) face both high exposure and low adaptive capacity, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles. Professional/managerial occupations (56.9M workers, AC=0.734) diverge sharply from administrative support (17.8M workers, AC=0.360) despite similar AI exposure levels.
keyFindings: Of 37.1 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million (71%) are in occupations with above-median adaptive capacity
6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) are both highly AI-exposed and in the bottom quartile of adaptive capacity, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles
AI exposure and adaptive capacity show a positive correlation of r=0.502 across 356 occupations

Professional and managerial occupations (56.9M workers) average adaptive capacity of 0.734 despite substantial AI exposure (0.400), while administrative support averages only 0.360 with the highest exposure of any major group (0.525)
Women make up approximately 81.3% of workers in high-vulnerability occupations (high exposure + low adaptive capacity) vs 48.0% in other occupations
methodology: Composite index from four components using employment-weighted Z-scores: (1) Net liquid wealth from SIPP 2022-2024 (log-transformed median), (2) Growth-weighted skill transferability from O*NET Skills and Work Activities with BLS 2024-2034 employment projections via cosine similarity, (3) Geographic density from Lightcast employment-weighted average log CBSA density, (4) Age from ACS fraction 55+. AI exposure from Eloundou et al. (2024) E1+0.5E2 estimates. Sample: 356 occupations meeting data quality thresholds across SIPP (>=15 respondents), OEWS, O*NET, ACS, Lightcast, and AI exposure data. KNN imputation (k=10, 0.92 correlation) for ~15% of occupations lacking O*NET skills data. Bootstrap 95% CI for correlation: [0.353, 0.624].
qualifiers: Adaptive capacity index measures occupation-level characteristics, not individual workers; within-occupation heterogeneity is masked. Neither the index nor AI exposure measures can predict displacement likelihood. Index uses equal component weighting for transparency though components may contribute unequally. Occupation-level aggregation from SIPP may be unreliable for small-sample occupations. Historical displacement cost evidence may not hold if AI fundamentally reshapes the economy. Geographic analysis excludes rural areas outside CBSAs. Only 4.9% of high-vulnerability workers hold bachelor's degree or higher vs 10.1% in other occupations.
